title: What If a Capsule Full of Sun Crashed in the Desert? In 2004 One Did, at 193 mph

scenes.text: What if a capsule full of Sun hit the desert at 193 miles an hour? That happened.
NASA's Genesis spent hundreds of days beyond the Moon, catching solar wind on more than 200 four-inch wafers.
On September 8, 2004, it came home over Utah. The parachutes never opened. Four switches had been installed upside down.
It hit the Dugway Proving Ground at 311 kilometres an hour and split open. All but one of the wafers shattered.
Scientists picked the fragments out of the mud. It took until 2010, but they got the required science out.
The result: Earth isn't made from the Sun's average mix, as the standard model assumed. A crash rewrote the recipe.

description:
What if a capsule carrying samples of the Sun crashed at 193 mph? On 8 September 2004, NASA's Genesis return capsule did, after its parachutes failed because four gravity switches had been installed upside down.
It hit Utah's Dugway Proving Ground at about 311 km/h and broke open, shattering all but one of its 200-plus solar-wind collector wafers, yet scientists recovered enough material to meet the mission's goals by 2010 and to show that Earth is not made of the solar nebula's average mix.
What should we run through next?
thumbnail_text: WHAT IF A SUN CAPSULE CRASHED?
first_comment: Four switches installed upside down ended years of collecting in seconds. What space mishap should we run through next?
